text.title: Spec Delta Failure Modes
text.summary: Six ways a delta damages the source of truth it exists to protect. All six are silent: every one of them produces a delta that reads perfectly well.

failure.symptom: References to an identifier resolve to nothing. Tests still pass because they were updated in the same pull request, but three older acceptance criteria now point at a section that no longer exists.
failure.cause: A rename was expressed as a `REMOVED` plus an `ADDED`. Both halves are individually valid and the reviewer had no way to know they were one operation.
failure.prevention: RENAMED with an explicit `old -> new` pair. It is a separate verb precisely because the delete-plus-add form is undetectable — to a reader and to a tool.

failure.symptom: A behaviour stops being tested and nobody notices for two releases. The test suite is green throughout.
failure.cause: A spec section was removed and the acceptance criteria hanging off it were never re-homed. The tests kept running against nothing in particular.
failure.prevention: Every REMOVED and CHANGED block enumerates what referenced it and where each reference went. `none` is allowed and must be verified, because it is a claim, not a default.

failure.symptom: Two documents describe the same rule differently, both look authoritative, and the newer one is not obviously the right one.
failure.cause: The delta copied a chunk of the baseline in for context, and the copy stopped tracking the original the moment either moved.
failure.prevention: Name the baseline by path and git ref; quote at most a line for context. A per-feature copy of the domain forks the source of truth by construction, which is why that layout was rejected outright.

failure.symptom: An added section carries an awkward identifier that nobody can explain, or a change silently vanished after merge.
failure.cause: Operations were applied in whatever order they appeared. An ADDED hit a collision with a section that was about to be removed, so the author renamed the new thing to get past it — permanently. Or a CHANGED applied to a section that a later REMOVED then deleted.
failure.prevention: `RENAMED → REMOVED → CHANGED → ADDED`, in the file and in application. Every other order makes at least one class of conflict either invisible or fake.

failure.symptom: The merged `project-spec/` is incoherent and diagnosing which operation caused it takes an afternoon of git archaeology.
failure.cause: The delta was moved to the archive as part of "closing the feature", before the merged spec was verified. The instruction set was gone at the moment it was needed.
failure.prevention: Merge, verify, then archive — and retain the archive. The sequence of deltas is the only reconstructable history of how the spec reached its current state.

failure.symptom: A long "Unchanged" section that nobody reads, is never complete, and is quietly wrong within one sprint. Reviewers stop trusting the whole file.
failure.cause: An attempt to reassure reviewers that omissions were deliberate, implemented as the complement of the delta over the entire baseline — a set that cannot be enumerated.
failure.prevention: `## Out of Scope` instead: the handful of adjacent things a reader would have expected to change, each one a decision somebody actually made. Bounded, verifiable, and worth the reviewer's attention.
